skill.name: Where a new paragraph starts
skill.why: Paragraphs show readers when something changes, so they don't get lost.
skill.how: Start a new paragraph when the time, place, topic or speaker changes.

beats.say: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one thing.
When the time changes, start a new paragraph.
beats.show: **The next morning,** the snow had gone.

beats.say: Start a new one when the place changes, too.
beats.show: **Back at the ship,** Mo was burning toast.

beats.say: A new topic gets a new paragraph.
beats.show: Wombats have strong claws. **Wombat poo** is shaped like a cube.

beats.say: And every new speaker gets a new paragraph.
beats.show: 'Who ate my pie?' asked Tully. **'Not me,' said Mo.**

encounters.text: Every spring, billions of bogong moths fly up to the Australian Alps. Some travel more than a thousand kilometres to get there. They fly at night, and scientists think they use the stars and the Earth's magnetic field to find their way. When they arrive, they squeeze into cool, dark cracks between the boulders. Thousands of moths can pack into a single square metre of rock, like a furry brown carpet. They stay there all summer, resting, and then fly home in autumn. Bogong moths are also an important food for many animals on the mountain. Mountain pygmy possums fatten up on them after waking from their long winter sleep. Ravens pick them out of the cracks with their beaks. Even foxes have been seen licking moths off the rocks like lollies.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote about her first sea dragon. The Ledgeling has never seen the sea.
encounters.text: Wren had always wanted to see a weedy sea dragon, and today was her chance. She rolled backwards off the dive boat and sank slowly through the cold green water. Below her, the kelp swayed like a forest in the wind. She swam between the long brown fronds, searching every shadow. For twenty minutes, she saw nothing but a grumpy crab. Then, just as her air was running low, something moved. A sea dragon, no longer than a ruler, drifted out from the kelp, its leafy fins fluttering. Wren hovered perfectly still and watched it for as long as she possibly dared, holding her breath. Back on the boat, she peeled off her mask and burst into happy tears. encounters.text: Every evening after school, Tully went down to the frozen oval at the bottom of Scaffold Peaks to practise kicking. Her goal was simple: to make the Reef Rays junior squad, the team she had supported since she was four years old. She set up a row of witches' hats along the boundary and tried to kick the ball between them from fifty metres out. Most of her kicks sailed wide, and one bounced off a seagull, who was not impressed. Her fingers went numb inside her gloves, and her breath came out in clouds. Still, she kept a notebook in her pocket and wrote down every single kick, the good ones and the terrible ones, until the floodlights switched off at seven. Six months later, on the same frozen oval, Tully kicked her hundredth goal in a row without missing once. The Reef Rays coach, who had been watching quietly from the fence, wrote something in a notebook of her own. Then she walked over and handed Tully an envelope with the club's logo on the front.

He promised himself that one day he would ride a rocket like that one, heading somewhere nobody had ever been. He fell asleep on the roof, still holding the telescope, and his mum had to carry him inside. Thirty years later, Commander Kip Ferreira stood at the window of the first ship ever to orbit Mars.
